definition.text: A natural mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms that together support the life of plants and soil organisms; all of Earth's soil together is called the pedosphere.

facts.text: Soil joins a solid matrix of minerals and organic matter with pores holding gases (the soil atmosphere) and water with dissolved substances (the soil solution): a three-state system.
It is a product of climate, relief, organisms and parent material interacting over time, and it keeps developing through physical, chemical and biological processes, including weathering and erosion.
Most soils have a dry bulk density of 1.1 to 1.6 g/cm3, while the soil particles themselves are much denser, at 2.6 to 2.7 g/cm3.
Little of Earth's soil is older than the Pleistocene and none is older than the Cenozoic, though fossilized soils survive from as far back as the Archean.
Soil has four important functions: a medium for plant growth; water storage, supply and purification; a modifier of Earth's atmosphere; and a habitat for soil organisms.
A gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species, mostly microbial and largely unexplored, and soil ecologists regard soil as an ecosystem.
Soil is an important carbon reservoir in Earth's carbon cycle, and potentially one of the most reactive to human disturbance and climate change.
Some scientific definitions reserve the word dirt for displaced soil.

definition.text: The proportions of solids (minerals and organic matter) and of pore space, shared between water and air, that make up a soil.

facts.text: A typical soil is about 50% solids (45% mineral and 5% organic matter) and 50% pores, half occupied by water and half by gas.
In the short term the mineral and organic shares stay constant, while water and gas trade places: a rise in one is balanced by a fall in the other.
Pore space lets air and water enter and move, both critical for soil life; compaction, especially under heavy machinery, shrinks it and keeps air and water from roots and organisms.
Mineral particles interacting with organic matter, water and gases flocculate into aggregates or peds; where these can be identified, the soil is said to be developed.
Most nutrients are held by clay and organic colloids: adsorbed on clay surfaces, bound inside clay minerals, or locked in living organisms and humus.
Apart from nitrogen fixed from the atmosphere, most plant nutrients originate in the minerals of the parent material.
Biological influences on soil properties are strongest near the surface, while geochemical influences increase with depth.

title: Soil solution

definition.text: The water held in soil pores together with the many organic and mineral substances dissolved or suspended in it.

facts.text: Because soil water is never pure but carries hundreds of dissolved organic and mineral substances, it is more accurately called the soil solution.
Its dissolved substances, organic and inorganic, occur in ionic or molecular form in the liquid phase of the soil.
Water drives the dissolution, precipitation and leaching of minerals in the profile, making it a critical agent of soil development.
Nutrients bound to clay and organic matter buffer the solution's composition as soils wet and dry, plants take up nutrients, salts are leached or acids and alkalis are added.
Soil pH measures the hydrogen ion activity in the soil solution and affects how available plant nutrients are.

notes: No own article or section; passes the 2+ pages test (Soil, Plant nutrients in soil, Alkali soil, Leaching (agriculture), Agricultural soil science).

title: What counts as soil

definition.text: The unsettled question of where soil ends and other loose surface material begins, in particular whether lifeless regolith can be called soil.

facts.text: One classic definition says soil has formed once organic matter accumulates and washed-down colloids leave a distinct B horizon.
That definition is somewhat arbitrary, since mixtures of sand, silt, clay and humus support biological and farming activity before a B horizon forms.
Twentieth-century thinking cast soil as earthy material altered by living processes; on that view, soil without a living component is simply part of Earth's outer layer, a regolith.
More recent definitions embrace soils without any organic matter, such as regoliths formed on Mars and in comparable Earth deserts.
Calling the surface material of the Moon and Mars soil is accepted by only part of the scientific community.
In engineering terms, soil is simply part of regolith, the loose material above bedrock, as also found on the Moon and other celestial bodies.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether material without life or organic matter, such as Martian or lunar regolith, should be called soil.

definition.text: The many ways people rely on soil, from growing food and fibre to construction, mining and landscape work.

facts.text: In agriculture soil anchors plants and is their primary nutrient base; the soil type and available moisture determine which plants can be grown.
Soil resources produce 98.8% of the food humans consume.
Soil is the foundation for most construction and the basis of many building materials; surface mining, road building and dam construction move massive volumes of it.
Waste treatment relies on soil: septic drain fields and land application of wastewater use aerobic soil processes, and landfills use soil as daily cover.
Water percolating through soil to become groundwater is filtered of pollutants such as pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals and excess nutrients.
Organic soils, especially peat, are a significant fuel and horticultural resource, and drained peatlands are farmed in Nordic countries.
Geophagy, eating soil-like substances, is practised by animals and humans; some monkeys eat soil with their foliage to ease tannin toxicity.
Aeroponics, aquaponics and hydroponics show that soil is not strictly essential for agriculture.

definition.text: Improving degraded or badly balanced soils by adding materials such as clay, gypsum, sand, organic matter or biochar.

facts.text: Soils rich in swelling smectite clays are often very fertile: the smectite-rich paddy soils of Thailand's Central Plains are among the world's most productive.
On low-clay soils in Thailand, adding bentonite clay once at 200 kilograms per rai (1,300 kg/ha) raised yields by an average of 73% in field trials.
Soils too high in clay or salts can be balanced with gypsum, washed river sand and organic matter; sandy, nutrient-poor soils benefit from compost or ramial chipped wood.
Biochar is used to improve nutrient-poor tropical soils, modelled on fertile Amazonian Dark Earths, though uncontrolled use of charred wastes may endanger soil life and human health.

definition.text: The outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil and subject to soil formation and erosion.

facts.text: It lies at the interface of the lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere, and develops only where all four interact dynamically.
The pedosphere is the foundation of terrestrial ecosystems and mediates chemical and biogeochemical fluxes into and out of the other spheres.
It lies within the Critical Zone, a wider interface running from vegetation through aquifers and regolith down into bedrock.
Soil formation begins with the chemical or physical breakdown of minerals over bedrock; it can start without life but is greatly quickened by biological reactions.
Over time the soil's bulk chemistry drifts away from that of the bedrock toward one reflecting the reactions taking place in the soil.
The chemistry of the underlying rock sets the primary conditions for soil development, and few rock types locally enrich limiting elements such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
Soil formation is dominated by chemical weathering of silicate minerals, aided by acids from pioneer organisms and by carbonic acid from the atmosphere.

definition.text: The first colonisers of bare rock, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, whose acids begin turning rock into soil.

facts.text: Biological inputs may begin with lichens and other microorganisms, including cyanobacteria, green algae, fungi and bacteria, that secrete oxalic acid.
Lichens have long been seen as the pioneers of soil, yet seed-bearing plants can colonise faster; lichens tolerate harsher conditions and dominate in alpine regions.
Organic acids from roots and decay, such as citric, phenolic, humic and fulvic acids, speed chemical weathering by chelation.
As the soil thickens, earthworms, burrowing mammals and large animals above ground go on altering its chemistry and fertility.

definition.text: What the pedosphere receives from the air, mainly wind-blown sediment, rainfall and diffusing gases.

facts.text: Eolian (wind-borne) sedimentation carries aerosols, pollen and dust particles into soils.
After water, nitrogen is the most abundant constituent of rain, because water vapour uses aerosol particles to form droplets.
Carbon dioxide from roots and microbes keeps soil-water bicarbonate far above equilibrium with the air, which together with dissolved metals lowers soil pH.
Gases escaping from soil to the atmosphere come from carbonate dissolution, decomposition, redox reactions and microbial photosynthesis.

definition.text: Soils formed under forest, usually well developed with thick humus layers.

facts.text: In forests precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration, so surplus water percolates down through the soil layers.
Slow decomposition releases much fulvic acid, which greatly enhances chemical weathering.
Percolating water and weathering leach magnesium, iron and aluminium downward (podzolization), giving marked contrasts in colour and chemistry between layers.
Forest soils can form a thick soil carbon sponge.

definition.text: Soils of tropical forests, which receive more sunlight and rain over longer growing seasons than any other environment.

facts.text: Tropical biomass is extremely productive, producing as much as 800 grams of carbon per square meter per year (8 tons of C/hectare/year).
Heat and abundant water raise rates of chemical weathering, while fast decomposition leaves less fulvic acid to leach metals.
Unlike temperate forest soils, they show little or no podzolization and lack marked visual and chemical contrasts between layers.
Mobile magnesium, iron and aluminium instead precipitate as oxide minerals, giving the soil a rusty red colour.

definition.text: Soils formed where precipitation equals or falls short of evapotranspiration, so that soil development works under drought.

facts.text: Limited downward percolation of water and organic acids reduces leaching, chemical weathering and soil development.
Evaporation builds up calcium, which with other large cations flocculates clay minerals and fulvic acids in the upper profile.
With little leaching, calcium precipitates as calcite in lower layers to form caliche; in deserts a layer of gypsum and halite may lie beneath it.
The depth of maximum clay concentration increases where precipitation and leaching are greater.

title: Soil science

definition.text: The study of soil as a natural resource: its formation, classification and mapping, its physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and how these bear on soil use and management.

facts.text: Its two main historical branches are pedology, the study of soil in its natural setting, and edaphology, the study of soil in relation to the uses that depend on it.
Both branches combine soil physics, soil chemistry and soil biology, and academic soil scientists tend to specialise in biology, pedology, edaphology, physics or chemistry.
Engineers, agronomists, chemists, geologists, ecologists, microbiologists, archaeologists and planners all add to knowledge of soils.
Soil occupies the pedosphere, one of the spheres the geosciences use to organise the Earth conceptually.
New research is driven by climate change, greenhouse gases and carbon sequestration, and by interest in biodiversity and in past cultures.
Soil scientists are concerned about preserving soil and arable land as population, food consumption and land degradation grow.
In 1998 the World Reference Base for Soil Resources replaced the FAO soil classification as the international system; its current 4th edition dates from 2022.
Soil mapping classifies soil types and properties in an area and geo-encodes them, increasingly through digital methods using remote sensing.

related: World Reference Base for Soil Resources

definition.text: The view, developed by Dokuchaev, that soil is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it.

facts.text: Fallou and Dokuchaev are both credited as among the first to treat soil as a resource distinct from geology and crop production; Fallou came first, but Dokuchaev's work proved more significant.
Before them, soil was seen as a product of chemical transformations of rocks, a dead substrate from which plants draw nutrients.
For Dokuchaev, rock becomes soil under soil-forming factors: climate, vegetation, country, relief and age.
A 1914 encyclopedic definition, forms of earth formed by the weathering of rocks, shows how long the older view persisted.
In the 20th century the concept became one of earthy material altered by living processes, and it is still being refined to take in energy transport within soil.
Nikiforoff's 1959 definition of soil as the 'excited skin of the sub aerial part of the Earth's crust' fits this modern understanding.

definition.text: Folk systems that name soils either with unique names or by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy.

facts.text: They tell soils apart by appearance (colour, texture, landscape position), performance (production capability, flooding) and the vegetation growing on them.
A familiar vernacular distinction is between heavy (clayey) and light (sandy) soils.
Light soils are easier to cultivate and resist compaction by trampling cattle but erode more easily; they are not lower in bulk density or more porous than heavy soils.
The earliest known soil classification, in the Chinese Yu Gong (5th century BCE), sorted soil into three categories and nine classes by colour, texture and hydrology.

definition.text: The practical work of soil scientists, traditionally mapping soils and increasingly addressing land and environmental problems across disciplines.

facts.text: Almost every area of the United States has a published soil survey, with tables on how soil properties support or limit uses.
Landscape tasks include protecting environmentally critical areas and valuable habitats, managing land for productivity and remediating damaged lands.
Less obvious applications include dating past activity at a site, reading archaeological stratification, vitrifying radioactive waste and using soil microbes to degrade contaminants.
The Critical Zone concept gives a framework for cross-disciplinary research on soil, rock, air, water and living resources at Earth's surface.

definition.text: The branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve and builds frameworks for describing soil bodies, often in their natural environment.

facts.text: It is one of two main branches of soil inquiry; the other, edaphology, is more agronomic and studies how soil properties influence plant communities.
Pedologists observe soil morphology, where soils occur and how they fit into wider contexts of time and space, and from this build classifications, soil maps and theories.
Its sub-disciplines include pedometrics, the quantitative characterisation and mapping of soils, and soil geomorphology, which links landform processes with soil formation.
Agronomists once saw soil as a static production medium while pedologists studied its relation to landscape history; the two approaches are now integrated.
As a soil forms, its profile slowly deepens and develops characteristic layers called horizons while it approaches a steady state.
Fallou conceived pedology in the 19th century as a fundamental science separate from agrology, the applied forerunner of edaphology.

definition.text: The working principles pedologists use to explain soil genesis, starting from the idea that external factors drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns.

facts.text: Complexity in soil genesis is more common than simplicity, and today's soils carry imprints of past processes that may be hard to observe or measure.
Five major external factors (climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time) plus smaller ones drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns.
Soil-forming processes both create and destroy order within soils, often at once; the profile records the balance of these processes, present and past.
Uniformitarianism applies to soils: today's soil-forming processes have run since organisms first appeared on land, though with varying intensity in space and time.
Few soils are geologically old: most soils and land surfaces are no older than the Pleistocene, though lithified paleosols occur through most of geologic time.
Soils are natural clay factories; much of the world's shale is soil clay eroded into ocean basins and later lithified.
Knowing soil genesis aids classification, mapping and management, but classifications cannot rest on genesis alone, since processes are seldom observed and change over time.

definition.text: The branch of soil science concerned with the influence of soils on living things, especially plants.

facts.text: It is one of the two main divisions of soil science alongside pedology, and covers how soil shapes people's use of land for plant growth and other purposes.
Its general subfields are agricultural soil science (agrology in some regions) and environmental soil science.
Pedology and edaphology were at first poorly distinguished: Russian soil scientists used edaphology as a synonym of pedology, and Spanish ones preferred it.
Driven out of pedology-centred soil science in the 20th century, edaphology is now recognised as a necessary branch complementary to pedology.
Xenophon and Cato were early edaphologists; Cato recommended tillage, crop rotation and legumes to build soil nitrogen, and devised the first soil capability classification for crops.
Environmental soil science covers vadose zone functions, septic fields, wastewater and stormwater, erosion control, contamination and remediation, wetland restoration and nutrient management.

conflicts.note: Soil#Studies of soil fertility gives Xenophon's dates as 450–355 BCE; Edaphology#History gives 431–355 BC.

definition.text: An experiment in which Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil for five years, supplying only rainwater.

facts.text: The weight the tree gained exceeded the weight the soil lost.
Van Helmont concluded that the willow was made of water; only partly correct, the experiment reignited interest in edaphology.

definition.text: The ways industrialised production and farming have changed how soils interact with plants.

facts.text: Increased mechanical production has raised heavy metal levels in soils, and these metals have also been found in crops.
Greater use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides has decreased the nutrient availability of soils.
Monocropping lowers biodiversity, which reduces the nutrients available in soils, and increases dependency on chemical fertilizer.
Intensive tillage disturbs soil microbial communities that help maintain soil moisture and air circulation.

title: Earthworks (engineering)

definition.text: Engineering works created by moving or processing quantities of soil or unformed rock.

facts.text: Typical earthworks include roads, railway beds, causeways, dams, levees, canals and berms, and grading land to reshape a site or stabilise slopes.
Military earthworks, from moats and hill forts to trenches, exploit soil that is not very strong but cheap enough to use in huge quantities.
Engineers weigh soil density and strength and match cut volumes to fill volumes over minimal distances, since cost is hauled amount times hauled distance.
Earthwork construction was revolutionised by the Fresno scraper and machines such as the loader, dump truck, grader, bulldozer, backhoe and dragline excavator.

notes: curriculum review: civil engineering, not soil science

definition.text: A raised wall, bank or mound of earth or stone built to hold back water or carry a roadway.

facts.text: Roads, railways and aqueducts are raised on embankments of compacted soil, typically clay or rock-based, to avoid changes in level; cuttings serve where the land is too high.
Embankments are often built from material dug out of cuttings, and need compacted, waterproofed material for long-term stability.
A sand-bentonite mixture is one embankment material, often used to protect underground cables and pipelines.

definition.text: A construction material made of pulverised natural soil mixed with a little Portland cement and water and compacted to high density.

facts.text: Cement hydration gives a hard, semi-rigid material with good compressive and shear strength but low tensile strength, so it is prone to cracking.
Unlike concrete, it has too little cement paste to coat every particle, leaving voids and a cement matrix with nodules of uncemented material.
It is used for pipe bedding, slope protection and road subbases; soil-cement bases can be thinner than granular ones and grow stronger with age.
Cement-modified soils use less cement to upgrade a poor soil, lowering plasticity and volume change and raising bearing ratio and shear strength.

definition.text: A structure, usually a house, with soil against its walls or on its roof, or built entirely underground.

facts.text: The surrounding earth acts as thermal mass, keeping indoor temperature steady and cutting heating and cooling costs.
Earth sheltering is one of the oldest forms of building; migratory hunters in Europe are thought to have insulated sunken huts with turf and earth from about 15,000 BC.
The three main types are bermed, with earth banked against outer walls; in-hill, set into a slope with earth on the roof; and true underground, set below grade.
Earth sheltering became relatively popular after the mid-1970s, especially among environmentalists.

title: Fresno scraper

definition.text: A horse-drawn machine for building canals and ditches in sandy soil, the model for most modern earthmoving scrapers.

facts.text: James Porteous invented it in 1883 to dig irrigation canals and ditches in the sandy soil of California's Central San Joaquin Valley.
Earlier scrapers pushed soil ahead; the Fresno lifted it into a C-shaped bowl and dumped it at a controlled depth, quadrupling the volume that could be moved by hand.
Its design influenced modern bulldozer blades and earth movers, and it served in farming, grading and building the Panama Canal.
In 1991 the American Society of Mechanical Engineers named it an International Historic Engineering Landmark.

notes: A machine rather than a soil concept; passes the own-article test only.; curriculum review: a tool, assigned by the graph

title: Aeroponics

definition.text: Growing plants in air or mist, with no soil or aggregate medium.

facts.text: Plants hang in a closed or semi-closed chamber while their roots and lower stems are sprayed with an atomised, nutrient-rich water solution.
It counts as a form of hydroponics, since water delivers the nutrients.
Air around the roots supplies the oxygen the root zone needs, and keeping plants apart limits the spread of disease.
In 1911 V.M. Artsikhovski described studying roots by spraying substances into the surrounding air, the method now called aeroponics.

notes: curriculum review: soilless growing, assigned by the graph

definition.text: The distance across a body of rock such as a bed or seam, measured at right angles to its surface.

facts.text: Originally a mining term for the workability of seams, it is used in soil science for the vertical extent of soil horizons.
Soil horizons differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries.
Digging another hole just ten metres away can reveal very different horizon depths and thicknesses.

definition.text: The near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact to regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources.

facts.text: It sustains nearly all terrestrial life and extends through the pedosphere, the unsaturated vadose zone and the saturated groundwater zone.
Critical Zone science integrates landscape evolution, weathering, hydrology, geochemistry and ecology across spatial and time scales and human influence.
These processes govern the mass and energy exchanges behind biomass production, chemical cycling and water storage.
Tsakalotos coined 'critical zone' in chemistry in 1909; Gail Ashley applied it in 1998 to the connection of vegetation to soil and weathered materials.
It is studied at Critical Zone Observatories, for which the US National Science Foundation sought proposals in 2006.
In practice the critical zone essentially equates to the pedosphere, while the biomantle is its uppermost, biota-rich layer.
It ends at some depth in bedrock, where life and water cease to change the chemistry significantly.

title: Soil health

definition.text: The state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as appropriate to its environment.

facts.text: Put simply, soil health arises from favorable interactions of all soil components, living and non-living, such as microbiota, plants and animals.
It depends on soil biodiversity and can be improved by keeping protective living covers on the soil and adding natural, carbon-containing amendments.
Inorganic fertilizers need not harm soil health if they are not used in excess and if they boost plant growth that returns more carbon-containing residues.
The term spans sustaining plant and animal productivity, enhancing biodiversity, maintaining water and air quality, and supporting human health and habitation.
Its underlying principle is that soil is a living, dynamic, ever-changing environment, not the inert growing medium that intensive farming tends to assume.
Soils highly fertile for crops are also biologically lively; temperate grassland soils hold 1–2 t/ha of bacterial and 2–5 t/ha of fungal biomass.
Some microbiologists believe that 80% of soil nutrient functions are essentially controlled by microbes.
By analogy with human health, a healthy soil is in biological, chemical and physical well-being, is not degraded, resists degradation and keeps cycling nutrients, carbon and water.

contested_note: A soil can be healthy for ecosystem functioning without directly serving crop production, so sources describe a scientific debate on its terms and measurement.
notes: The contested point is S:aecf861ce005; the Interpretations of soil health entry treats it in full.

definition.text: The condition of a soil judged by its capacity to perform ecosystem services that meet the needs of human and non-human life.

facts.text: It reflects how well a soil maintains biodiversity and productivity, partitions water and solute flow, filters and buffers, cycles nutrients and supports plants and structures.
Unlike water or air, which have established standards, soil quality is difficult to define or quantify.
Soil management has a major impact on soil quality; cover crops, for example, raise it by adding organic matter over time.
Soil organisms contribute to soil quality in countless ways, and the amount and diversity of the biota appears proportional to it.
Arbuscular mycorrhizae help host plants establish on degraded soil and improve its quality and health.

title: Soil functions

definition.text: The general capabilities of soils that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses.

facts.text: They include functions for natural ecosystems, agricultural productivity, environmental quality, as a source of raw materials and as a base for buildings.
For food and biomass production, soil stores and supplies nutrients, exchanges CO2 for fresh O2 in the root zone, holds water in its pores and moderates temperature.
Soil is a biological habitat and gene reserve for many organisms, and it turns the remains of dead plants and animals into simpler mineral forms other life can use.
Soil supplies raw materials and shapes human health, since food reflects the soil it grew in; Maya ceramics, for example, inherited traits from the soils used to make them.
Productive soil is limited in area, so with growing pressure from cropping, forestry and urbanization, extracting soil as a raw material needs to be controlled.
As cultural heritage, soil gives a sense of place, preserves artifacts of the past and has guided where people settle.
About 50% of people live in houses built from soil, and roads and buildings resting on it depend on its bearing strength, compressibility, stability and shear strength.
